title: Serving through the body
hookLine: eating, working and resting can be worship

lines: THE SANDWICH CAN BE WORSHIP TOO.
cards: Where does worship happen? The easy answer is a building. A sanctuary, an ark, rows of seats, a quiet hour set apart from the rest of the week.
And then there's everything else: the sandwich at your desk, the dishes, the shift at work, the nap on the couch. Two lists. Holy over here, ordinary over there.
The Hasidic teachers looked at those two lists and refused to keep them apart. The sandwich, they said, can be worship too. Not instead of prayer, but alongside it.
Today's word is the name for that refusal.

teach.b: Avodah b'gashmiyut. Avodah is service, worship, the same word once used for the service in the Temple. Gashmiyut is physicality, the stuff of the body and the material world.
Service through the physical. First, the verse.
Proverbs says, "In all thy ways acknowledge Him, and He will direct thy paths." Hasidic teachers leaned hard on the word all. Not only in the ways that look religious.
In all of them. Second, the older roots. The Mishnah in Pirkei Avot teaches that all your deeds should be for the sake of Heaven.

teach.h: A PERSON'S TABLE, LIKE AN ALTAR.
teach.b: And the Talmud makes a bold comparison: while the Temple stood, the altar brought atonement, and now a person's table does. The kitchen table, set with food and with guests, takes up some of the altar's work.
Third, the Hasidic turn. If God is present everywhere, then a meal eaten with a blessing before it and attention during it isn't a break from serving God. It's a way of serving.
Working honestly, resting on the Sabbath, sleeping so you can rise and do good: all of it can be avodah, when it's done with the right intention. Fourth, the caution.
This is not permission to call every appetite holy.
The point isn't that whatever the body wants is worship. It's that the body, used with intention, can become a place where worship happens. Two lists become one.

how: Observant Jews say a blessing before and after eating, and Hasidic teaching asks that ordinary acts like eating, working and sleeping be done with the intention of serving God.

o: a rule to fast before every holy day
serving God through eating, working and resting
the priests' daily work in the ancient Temple

games.q: serve through the body — tap the pairs.
p: in all thy ways acknowledge Him
a person's table, like an altar

s: this teaching says whatever the body wants is holy
the point is the body used with intention, not every appetite.
the Talmud compares a person's table to the altar
while the Temple stood, the altar brought atonement; now a person's table does.
serving through the body replaces prayer
it sits alongside prayer: the ordinary becomes another place of service.

games.q: you're about to eat lunch at your desk. a Hasidic teacher asks what this meal is.
o: a possible way of serving God, if done with intention.
games.why: for them, a meal eaten with a blessing and attention isn't a break from service. it's service.

practice: Think ahead to the next thing you'll eat, and see yourself pausing before the first bite: a blessing said slowly if you say one, or simply noticing where the food came from, the ground, the rain, the hands that grew it and cooked it.
For now, sit with that plan, and with the plain fact of your body breathing.

wordCard.voice: Avodah b'gashmiyut. Service through the physical: the Hasidic teaching that eating, working and resting, done with intention, can be worship. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: service through physicality. Avodah also names the service in the Temple.

carryVoice: Your line: serve through the body. Two lists can become one. Same time tomorrow.
